title: Irregular Plural Nouns
keyIdea: A plural noun names more than one. Regular nouns add s or es (cat, cats; fox, foxes). Irregular nouns do not follow that rule. Some change the letters inside: foot becomes feet, tooth teeth, goose geese, man men and mouse mice. Some add en: child becomes children and ox oxen. Some stay the same: one sheep, two sheep; one deer, two deer. Never add s to an irregular plural as well: mice, not mouses or mices. A collective noun is one word for a whole group, like a flock of birds or a pack of wolves.
familyTip: Play 'One, two!' in the car or at dinner. You say 'one mouse', and your child answers 'two mice'. Mix regular nouns (one dog, two dogs) with irregular ones (foot, tooth, child, goose, sheep, woman) so they have to listen, not just add s. When you hear 'mouses' or 'foots', say the right form back in a sentence rather than correcting: 'Yes, two mice ran away!' Then name groups together: a flock of birds, a herd of cows, a swarm of bees.

visual.caption: How does each noun make its plural? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: test if s works, swap letters inside, sort irregular families, catch mouses and tooths, name groups.

kid: A noun names a person, animal or thing. Plural means more than one. Most nouns just add s: one cat, two cats. Words that end in s, x, sh or ch add es: one fox, two foxes.
Some nouns break the rule. They are irregular. Instead of adding s, they change the letters inside. One foot, two feet. One tooth, two teeth. One goose, two geese. One mouse, two mice.
Other irregular nouns add en, like one child, two children. And some do not change at all: one sheep, two sheep, one deer, ten deer.

Watch out for two slips. Do not add s to a noun that is irregular: say mice, not mouses. And do not add s to a word that is already plural: say children, not childrens. A word like flock or herd names a whole group. It is called a collective noun.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. The National Curriculum in England (English Appendix 1, Years 1 and 2) teaches the regular plural suffixes -s and -es; Common Core L.2.1b asks second graders to form and use frequently occurring irregular plural nouns (feet, children, teeth, mice, fish), and L.2.1a to use collective nouns (group). Key terms: noun, singular, plural, regular plural, irregular plural, suffix, collective noun.

Irregular plurals in everyday English fall into a few small families that come from Old English. Vowel change (umlaut plurals): foot to feet, tooth to teeth, goose to geese, man to men, woman to women, mouse to mice, louse to lice. The -en plural: child to children, ox to oxen. Zero plurals, where singular and plural look the same: sheep, deer, many fish names. Because there is no rule that predicts which nouns are irregular, children learn them as a list, then check by saying 'one ..., two ...' aloud.

Common mistakes: over-regularising, which is a normal stage of learning, so children say mouses, foots, tooths, childs and sheeps; double marking, where s is added to a form that is already plural (feets, childrens, mices, womens); writing the singular after a number (three goose); and mixing up collective nouns, such as a pack of birds. Be careful with possessives later: children's and women's take apostrophe s because the plural does not end in s.

In the lab your child sorts six nouns into 'just add s' or 'the word changes', drags ee, e or ice into the middle of foot, tooth, goose, man and mouse, sorts six irregular nouns into the change-inside, add-en and stays-the-same families, finds the wrong plural in five sentences, and drags flock, pack, herd or swarm into a gap for four groups of animals. Every wrong move gets a reason, such as 'That word is already plural'.

practice.hint: tooth is irregular. Say it out loud: one tooth, two …
practice.explain: teeth. The oo inside changes to ee, and no s is added.

practice.prompt: There are {n} sheep in a field. {k} more sheep join them. How many sheep are there now?
practice.hint: Add the sheep together. The word sheep stays the same for one or many.
practice.explain: {n} sheep and {k} more make {=n+k} sheep. We still write sheep, not sheeps.

practice.hint: child is irregular, and children is already plural.
practice.explain: children is the plural of child. Do not add s to it as well.

practice.prompt: Each child has 2 feet. How many feet do {n} children have?
practice.explain: {n} children with 2 feet each have {=2*n} feet. feet is the plural of foot.

practice.prompt: A group of birds is called a ___ of birds.
practice.hint: Think of birds flying together, or a group of sheep in a field.
practice.explain: a flock of birds. pack is for wolves and herd is for cows.

pool.hint: mouse is irregular. It changes inside.
pool.explain: mice. mouse changes inside, and mice is already plural, so it takes no s.

pool.prompt: Which noun just adds s to make its plural?
pool.hint: Say one …, two … for each word.
pool.explain: book is regular: books. goose becomes geese and man becomes men.

pool.prompt: Which word is wrong? Two womans walked to the shop.
pool.explain: womans should be women. woman changes inside, like man to men.

pool.hint: Some nouns stay the same for one or many.
pool.explain: deer stays the same: five deer.

pool.prompt: There are {n} geese on a pond. {k} geese fly away. How many geese are left?
pool.hint: Take away the geese that fly off.
pool.explain: {n} geese take away {k} leaves {=n-k} geese. One goose, many geese.

pool.hint: Look at the end of each word.
pool.explain: ox adds en to make oxen. feet changes inside and sheep stays the same.

pool.prompt: A person has 32 adult teeth. How many teeth do {n} adults have?
pool.explain: {n} adults with 32 teeth each have {=32*n} teeth. teeth is the plural of tooth.

pool.prompt: A group of wolves is a ___ of wolves.
pool.hint: Think of dogs or wolves hunting together.
pool.explain: a pack of wolves. A swarm is for bees and a flock is for birds.

pool.prompt: Which sentence about feet is right?
pool.hint: foot changes inside. Do not add s.
pool.explain: feet is the plural of foot. foots and feets are both slips.
